title: Travel light (Mark 6:7–13)
hookLine: he sends them out two by two with a staff and no bag
carry: less in the bag, more trust

cards: The charger, the spare charger, the just-in-case sweater, snacks, a book that won't get read. A suitcase can hold every disaster a person can imagine.
Right after his own hometown turns him away, Jesus does something bold. He doesn't pull back. He multiplies.
He sends the twelve out, in pairs, to the villages, to do what he's been doing. And before they go, he gives them a packing list. It's very short.

teach.b: Here it is, in the old King James Bible: "take nothing for their journey, save a staff only; no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse: But be shod with sandals; and not put on two coats."
A staff for walking, sandals, one coat. That's it. A scrip was a traveler's bag for food.
No bag means no stockpiling: they'll eat what they're given, so they have to be received. That's the point.

teach.h: NO BAG, NO BREAD, NO MONEY.
teach.b: Travelers without supplies depend on hospitality.

When a house takes you in, Jesus tells them, stay there. Don't shop around for a better one. And if a place won't have you, shake the dust off your feet as you leave, as a testimony against them, and move on.
Why two by two? Mark doesn't say. Nobody walks alone that way, and the law of Moses says a matter is settled by two witnesses.
Mark says they preached that people should turn around and start again, drove out demons, and "anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them."

Later, the letter of James tells the sick to call the elders to anoint them with oil. Churches still do it, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians count it among the sacraments. One more detail: Mark lets them take a staff.
Matthew and Luke say, not even a staff. Readers explain the difference in different ways. Either way, the list is short on purpose.
Less in the bag means more need for each other, and more room for trust.

how: Many churches send people out in pairs to visit and serve, and many anoint the sick with oil; Catholic and Orthodox Christians count the anointing of the sick among the sacraments.

games.q: you're one of the twelve. you arrive in a village and one house takes you in, but a nicer one down the street is also open. what does Jesus say?
o: stay where you were first welcomed.
sleep outside to avoid owing anyone.
games.why: stay in the house that takes you in until you leave that place. no shopping around for better hospitality.

practice: Picture your bag, backpack, purse or pockets, and what you carry every day just in case. Then go deeper: a worry you pack every morning, a grudge, a plan B for a plan B.
Choose one thing, an object or a weight, that you could leave behind, and picture setting it down; if you pray, you can hand it to God.

wordCard.voice: Travel light. The twelve sent out in pairs with a staff, sandals and one coat, depending on welcome.

orig.note: Greek: a bag for provisions on the road. The King James calls it a scrip.

carryVoice: Your line: less in the bag, more trust. A staff, sandals, one coat, and a friend beside you. That's day one hundred eighty-one.
